question: What is the treatment for visually signiﬁcant calciﬁc band keratopathy?
explanation: Not all band keratopathy needs to be treated, but if it is symptomatic or visually signiﬁcant, the treatment is epithelial debridement followed by chelation with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA).

question: What phase of the immune response arc is constituted by the initial recognition, transport, and presentation of antigenic substances to the adaptive immune system?
explanation: Following ingestion of antigen, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) migrate via aﬀerent lymphatics to lymph nodes. In the APCs, enzymatic digestion of proteins within endocytic vesicles produces short amino acid chains of 7–11 amino acids: the antigenic epitopic fragments. Each antigenic fragment is combined with a groove-shaped HLA peptide residing on the APC surface, and this surface complex forms a unique epitope. The combination of peptide and HLA protein is recognized by the T-lymphocyte receptors CD4 and CD8. question: What uveitic condition is characterized by the appearance of blood vessels in the anterior chamber angle without formation of peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS)?
explanation: Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis [FHI] or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is a chronic, mild, and typically unilateral uveitis associated with secondary open-angle glaucoma. Fine blood vessels are seen in the angle; they bridge the angle structures but do not grow or cause ﬁbrosis like rubeotic vessels. Posner-Schlossman syndrome, or glaucomatocyclitic crisis, is characterized by recurrent episodes of mild, unilateral iritis with marked elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) into the 40-60 mm Hg range. With repeated episodes, secondary open-angle glaucoma may develop. As in Fuchs uveitis syndrome, PAS do not develop, but unlike in Fuchs uveitis syndrome, angle vessels are not seen in Posner- Schlossman syndrome. Synechiae are common in both VKH disease and juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

question: Where is the density of Langerhans cells highest in a healthy cornea?

options.D: not present in any portion of cornea

explanation: Langerhans cells (LCs) are important components of the immune system and play roles in antigen presentation, control of lymphoid cell traﬃc, diﬀerentiation of T lymphocytes, and induction of delayed hypersensitivity. In the conjunctiva and limbus, LCs are the only cells that constitutively express MHC class II molecules. LCs are present in the peripheral cornea, and any stimulation to the central cornea results in central migration of the peripheral LCs. There are typically no antigen-presenting cells found in either the central cornea or in the sclera in a healthy eye. LCs are typically found in vascularized areas, such as the conjunctiva and the limbus.

question: What ﬁnding is most likely in an eye with Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHIC; also called Fuchs uveitis syndrome or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) in the absence of prior surgery?
explanation: Diﬀuse stellate keratoprecipitates are typically seen in FHIC and do not follow the pattern of the Arlt triangle, but are rather diﬀusely spread over the endothelial surface (similar to many other viral uveitides; there is data in the literature that now suggests FHIC is likely to be Rubella- associated anterior uveitis, which would place FHIC in the viral uveitides category). The diﬀuse stellate KP of FHIC are not symptomatic and should not be treated with corticosteroids, as not only do they not respond to treatment, but corticosteroids will only raise the risk of cataract formation and a steroid-induced pressure response. Patients with FHIC are not at risk for acute pressure spikes, but are at risk for the development of chronic, secondary open-angle glaucoma (along with cataracts and ﬂoaters) and should be followed as glaucoma suspects. Patients with FHIC typically do not present with CME, especially in the absence of prior surgery. While patients with FHIC can form posterior synechiae AFTER cataract surgery, the question speciﬁcally asks about the presence of posterior BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What treatment is likely to resolve human T-lymphotropic virus type -1 (HTLV-1) -associated retinal vasculitis?
explanation: Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus endemic to Japan, the Caribbean Islands, and Central and South America. About 1% of uveitis cases in Japan are due to HTLV-1. HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), HTLV-1- associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paralysis (HAM/TSP), and HTLV-1 uveitis. Most cases of HTLV-1 uveitis (HU) are classiﬁed as intermediate uveitis (75%). Patients also present with keratopathy, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient with bilateral pars planitis who is being treated with mycophenolate mofetil exhibits recurrent uveitic macular edema (UME) in the right eye. The anterior chamber and vitreous are inactive with respect to inﬂammation in both eyes, yet the macular edema persists. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula demonstrates uveitic macular edema in the right eye, but the OCT image is otherwise unremarkable. What is the best initial choice in managing the macular edema in this patient?

options.A: discontinuation of mycophenolate mofetil and advancement of systemic therapy to cyclophosphamide for better control of the underlying uveitis
options.B: intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days

explanation: Uveitic macular edema is a frequent complication of uveitis and may occur even when inﬂammation is otherwise controlled. Optical coherence tomography of the macula can help identify contributing factors to the macular edema, such as vitreomacular traction. If there is prominent vitreomacular traction, a pars plana vitrectomy may be considered. In this case, however, although there is uveitic macular edema, the imaging is otherwise unremarkable. If there were persistently active intraocular inﬂammation that may be driving the uveitic macular edema, advancing a patient’s systemic therapy may be beneﬁcial. However, this patient’s intraocular inﬂammation is inactive. In addition, advancing therapy from an antimetabolite (mycophenolate mofetil) to an alkylating agent (cyclophosphamide) is not indicated, because alkylating agents are reserved for aggressive, sight- threatening causes of ocular inﬂammation due to their signiﬁcant side eﬀects. Similarly, intravenous methylprednisolone would not be indicated as the ﬁrst step in managing this patient’s macular edema, although such therapy can be used initially for robust intraocular inﬂammation that must be managed quickly and requires doses higher BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the fundus ﬁnding in congenital Zika virus infection?

options.C: retinal pigment mottling and chorioretinal atrophy

explanation: There have been no reports of uveitis associated with congenital infection. Observed ocular abnormalities include microphthalmia, cataract, glaucoma, iris coloboma, retinal pigment mottling, chorioretinal atrophy, and optic nerve hypoplasia or atrophy. No vaccine exists to prevent Zika at this time. Mosquito-borne transmission of ZIKV has been reported in the United States, and current prevention eﬀorts focus on education and mosquito control.

question: A patient from sub-Saharan Africa presents with mild anterior uveitis; papular skin lesions on the buttocks, waist, and shoulders; and conjunctival nodules. There is mild retinal pigment epithelial atrophy and a suggestion of optic atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Onchocerciasis is one of the leading causes of blindness ("river blindness") in Central America, South America, and sub-Saharan Africa. It is caused by the parasite Onchocerca volvulus and is transmitted by the black ﬂies of Simulium genus. The larvae develop into mature worms that migrate to the skin and form subcutaneous nodules. Any part of the eye, from the conjunctiva and cornea to the uvea and posterior segment, including the retina and optic nerve, may be involved. Microﬁlariae can even be observed swimming in the anterior chamber. The microﬁlariae migrate to the surface of the cornea, causing punctate keratitis, or sclerosing keratitis if the infection is chronic. Over time, the entire cornea may become opaque, thus leading to blindness. Mild to severe anterior uveitis, secondary glaucoma, and cataract may develop. Posterior segment ﬁndings may include early disruption of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), as well as pigment dispersion and atrophy. These may ensue in severe chorioretinal atrophy and optic atrophy. Behçet disease classically aﬀects young males who have a history of oral ulcers and have explosive inﬂammatory ocular response. HIV/AIDS retinopathy usually is characterized by microvascular changes, such as cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms, and telangiectasias, and later subsequently described with secondary opportunistic infections. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease presents as a panuveitis with a prodromal, uveitis, convalescent, and recurrent stage.

question: In a patient with uveitis and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), what mechanism of increased IOP is most likely to be reversed with aggressive use of corticosteroids?

options.A: angle closure due to peripheral anterior synechiae
options.B: decreased aqueous production by ciliary body
options.D: anterior rotation of ciliary body due to shallow choroidal eﬀusions

explanation: Of the answer choices provided, resolution of inﬂammatory anterior choroidal eﬀusions in the setting of corticosteroid therapy will often result in posterior rotation of the ciliary body (CB) back to its native state, relieving the patient of secondary angle closure. (Another scenario where corticosteroid therapy in the setting of uveitis and elevated IOP can help lower the IOP is when there is an associated "trabeculitis," oftentimes seen in viral anterior uveitides). Of course, cycloplegics should also be used when anterior rotation of the ciliary body is thought to be a cause of increased IOP. Elevated IOP due to synechial angle closure will not respond to corticosteroid therapy, nor will a steroid response (in fact, it will only get worse with continued corticosteroids). Decreased aqueous production by the CB is one of the reasons patients with uveitis tend to have lower-than-baseline IOPs; treatment with corticosteroids causes resolution of intraocular inﬂammation and typically results in elevation of IOP back to baseline in these patients.

question: What is the most likely ﬁnding in a person who is HLA-A29 positive?

options.B: ovoid, yellowish chorioretinal lesions distributed mostly around the optic nerve

explanation: While over 90% of patients with birdshot chorioretinopathy are positive for HLA-A29, most people who are HLA-A29 positive will never manifest birdshot chorioretinopathy and will have a normal eye examination. Approximately 8% of the general population in the US is positive for HLA-A29, and fewer than 1 in 10,000 individuals in the US will manifest birdshot chorioretinopathy. Patients with birdshot chorioretinopathy may have creamy, ovoid chorioretinal lesions, retinal vasculitis, or macular edema.

question: What type of macrophage expresses scavenging receptors but synthesizes very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines?
explanation: Resting macrophages are the classic scavenging cell, capable of phagocytosis and uptake of dead cell membranes, chemically modiﬁed extracellular protein (ie, acetylated or oxidized lipoproteins), sugar ligands, naked nucleic acids, and bacterial pathogens. Resting monocytes express at least 3 types of scavenging receptors but synthesize very low levels of proinﬂammatory cytokines. Scavenging can occur in the absence of inﬂammation. Primed macrophages are derived from resting macrophages that become primed by exposure to certain cytokines. Upon priming, these cells become positive for major histocompatibility (MHC) class II antigen and capable of functioning as antigen-presenting cells to T lymphocytes. Primed macrophages thus resemble dendritic cells. They can exit tissue sites by aﬀerent lymphatic vessels to reenter the lymph node. Activated macrophages are classically deﬁned as macrophages producing the full spectrum of inﬂammatory and cytotoxic cytokines; thus, they mediate and amplify acute inﬂammation, tumor killing, and major antibacterial activity. Epithelioid cells and giant cells represent diﬀerent terminal diﬀerentiations of the activated macrophage. Stimulated (or reparative) macrophages are partially activated and produce some inﬂammatory cytokines that contribute to ﬁbrosis and wound healing. $ A. 13% A. 13% B. 2% B. 2% C. 79% C. 79% D. 1% D. 1% Stop steroids. question: What treatment is most appropriate for active bilateral syphilitic panuveitis?
explanation: Intravenous penicillin is the treatment of choice for syphilitic uveitis, and the treatment regimen is the same as for neurosyphilis: 18 to 24 million units per day (MU/d) of aqueous penicillin G (PCN G) for 10 to 14 days. Desensitization and treatment with PCN or ceftriaxone can be considered for PCN-allergic patients.

question: A positive result on an indirect immunoﬂuorescence assay (IFA) or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for Borrelia burgdorferi in a patient with intermediate uveitis should prompt what action as the most appropriate next step?

options.A: institution of intravenous penicillin for 10 to 14 days
options.B: conﬁrmation of serological results with a Western blot
options.D: comparison of titer to standard curve to determine bacterial load

explanation: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends a 2-step protocol for the diagnosis of active or previous infection with Borrelia burgdorferi: ELISA for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and IgG, and if this result is positive, then Western immunoblot testing. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based testing can also be used. For patients with only ocular involvement (ie, without CNS or cardiac involvement), the route and duration of antibiotic treatment is not well established.

question: A 40-year-old man complains of painless, progressive blurring of vision in one eye. Examination reveals a low-grade iritis, diﬀuse iris transillumination without posterior synechiae, and a 3+ posterior subcapsular cataract. There are diﬀuse stellate keratic precipitates. What is the best choice of preoperative treatment for cataract surgery in this patient?

options.B: Treatment should begin with topical prednisolone acetate 1% drops, every 2 hours, until the uveitis is quiet.
options.C: Treatment should begin with systemic prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks prior to surgery.
options.D: Treatment should begin with topical triﬂuridine 1% drops, 9 times a day, for 2 weeks, prior to surgery.

explanation: Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is unilateral, and symptoms can be overlooked. Blurry vision and discomfort are reported. Typically, patients have diﬀuse iris stromal atrophy leading to heterochromia, diﬀuse white stellate keratic precipitates, anterior chamber and anterior vitreous cells, or cataract. The diagnosis is usually based on heterochromia, distribution of the keratic precipitates, and lack of posterior synechiae. This condition is usually unilateral, and symptoms vary from none to mild blurring and discomfort. The prognosis is good in most cases, although the inﬂammation can linger for years. Topical steroids can alleviate the inﬂammation, but typically do not resolve it. Aggressive treatment is not indicated in most of the cases. These patients do quite well with cataract surgery and generally no preoperative treatment is needed.

question: What HLA typing result would best support a diagnosis of birdshot retinochoroidopathy? Treatment should begin with systemic prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks prior to surgery. C.
explanation: The HLA-A29 gene is strongly associated with birdshot retinochoroidopathy, with a sensitivity of 96% and a speciﬁcity of 93%. HLA-B27–associated ocular inﬂammatory conditions include anterior uveitis, scleritis, and peripheral ulcerative keratitis, but 5% to 10% of normal unaﬀected patients are carriers of this gene. HLA-DR4 and HLA-B51 each have statistically signiﬁcant population associations with ocular inﬂammatory disease (DR4 with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease and B51 with Behçet), but the modest positive and negative predictive values preclude meaningful use in most clinical scenarios. 895b- f6997b437c94)  familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR)

question: What does the diﬀerential diagnosis of a 3-year-old child with hypopyon uveitis include?
explanation: Retinoblastoma is the most common malignant ocular tumor of childhood. In familial cases, it presents in the ﬁrst year of life or between ages 1 and 3 in sporadic unilateral cases. The most common initial sign is leukocoria, followed by strabismus, vitreous hemorrhage, hyphema, hypopyon, ocular/periocular inﬂammation, glaucoma, and proptosis. Occasionally, the malignant cells enter the anterior chamber and present as pseudohypopyon. Hypopyon in childhood is retinoblastoma, until proven otherwise. Retinal dysplasia, FEVR, Norrie disease, and Stickler syndrome do not present with hypopyon uveitis.

question: What is the ﬁrst-line treatment in patients with unilateral nodular anterior scleritis and no known systemic disease association?
explanation: Oral NSAIDs are ﬁrst-line therapy for nodular anterior scleritis, as long as infectious causes have been excluded and there are no contraindications to NSAID use. Topical corticosteroids will have minimal to no eﬀect in this setting, while oral corticosteroids and IMT are reserved for more severe cases and those refractory to oral NSAIDs.

question: An individual infected with the human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) has necrotizing retinitis. What test would be most helpful in making the diagnosis?

options.A: blood and urine cultures for herpes viruses
options.B: anterior chamber tap for polymerase chain reaction

explanation: Necrotizing retinitis in patients with HIV can be caused by herpes viruses (varicella zoster virus [VZV], cytomegalovirus [CMV], herpes simplex virus [HSV]). The diagnosis is made clinically, but intraocular ﬂuid analysis of aqueous or vitreous samples or retinal biopsy may be performed in cases in which the diagnosis is unclear. Intraocular antibody production can be computed using Goldmann-Witmer (GW) coeﬃcient. Polymerase chain reaction is the most sensitive, speciﬁc, and rapid mode of diagnosis for early initiation of appropriate therapy. Serum and urine testing for these agents may be contributory but not diagnostic of ocular infection.

question: A patient presents with bilateral snowballs and snowbanking. No retinal or choroidal lesions are seen. Results of an exhaustive systemic workup were negative. What ﬁndings would an ophthalmologist most likely see on ﬂuorescein angiography in the retinal periphery?
explanation: The major site of inﬂammation in intermediate uveitis is vitreous. "Snowballs" and "snowbanking" are common. Retinal phlebitis is a common occurrence and leads to the peripheral venous leakage seen on ﬂuorescein angiography. Anterior chamber cells can occur in adults (this is more common in children), but this reaction is very mild. Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a common cause of vision loss. Ischemia due to phlebitis and angiogenic stimuli from inﬂammation can result in neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage, including retinal detachment. Dalen-Fuchs nodules are seen in sympathetic ophthalmia, Vogt- Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, and sarcoidosis.

question: What is the cause of hypotony in chronic anterior uveitis?

options.A: prolonged use (> 6 months) of oral corticosteroids
options.B: decreased aqueous production from the ciliary body
options.C: posterior synechiae resulting in iris bombé

explanation: Dysfunction of the ciliary body may be a sequela of chronic inﬂammation; this may be due to ciliary body detachment induced by cyclitic membranes, reversible dysfunction due to inﬂammation, or permanent dysfunction in the setting of ciliary body atrophy.

question: A patient being treated for HLA- B27-associated uveitis is responding to topical steroids but develops elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) on the sixth day of therapy. What is the best next step in management?
explanation: Early in the course of all cases of uveitis, the ﬁrst priority is the control of intraocular inﬂammation, even if the IOP is high. The dosage and frequency of corticosteroid use should not be decreased prematurely. If there is elevated intraocular pressure at any time during the treatment of uveitis, ocular anti-hypertensive agents (such as brimonidine) should be employed as soon as possible. However, pilocarpine should be avoided in all uveitic cases because it is pro- inﬂammatory and may aggravate synechiae formation. Similarly, prostaglandin-analogues are also avoided initially as a ﬁrst-line treatment in uveitis-induced IOP elevation.

question: What inﬂammatory cell type dominates the inﬁltrate in acute bacterial infections?
explanation: Neutrophils are eﬃcient phagocytes that readily clear tissues and degrade ingested material. They act as important eﬀector cells through the release of granule products and cytokines. Neutrophils dominate the inﬁltrate in experimental models and clinical examples of active bacterial infections of the conjunctiva (conjunctivitis), sclera (scleritis), cornea (keratitis), and vitreous (endophthalmitis). + +

question: What is the best initial therapy for this patient's current condition?

options.A: discontinuation of oral valganciclovir and injection of intraocular triamcinolone 4 mg
options.B: pars plana vitrectomy with intravitreal injection of foscarnet
options.C: continuation of oral valganciclovir and starting systemic corticosteroids
options.D: discontinuation of antiretroviral treatment and starting systemic corticosteroids

explanation: This patient is likely exhibiting immune recovery uveitis associated with improvement of his CD4 T- lymphocyte count and ability to mount an inﬂammatory response to retinal cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigens. Such inﬂammation can be managed with systemic corticosteroids. The best answer choice listed is to continue oral valganciclovir and start systemic corticosteroids. Use of periocular steroids should proceed with caution, because there is a chance that there may be a recurrence of the CMV retinitis. Intraocular steroids should be avoided as a ﬁrst-line therapy for managing immune recovery uveitis. Certainly, if periocular steroids were to be considered, antivirals should be continued. There is no role for pars plana vitrectomy as a ﬁrst-line therapy for this patient. While there may be a signiﬁcant amount of vitreous debris associated with inﬂammation, a trial of systemic corticosteroids may preclude the development of signiﬁcant debris. Discontinuing antiretroviral therapy is not advisable, as the goal of therapy is to improve the CD4 T- lymphocyte count and decrease the patient’s overall risk for the development of opportunistic infections. + + $ 58% of respondents answered correctly. They can occur anywhere, including skin, bones, or internal organs. Gummatous syphilis remains the most uncommon type of tertiary syphilis. question: A patient presents with decreased vision in the right eye. The result of the fundus examination is seen in Figure 1. What is the most likely cause of decreased vision?
explanation: CNV within the macula is the main cause of decreased vision in OHS. CNV within choroidal scars develops in approximately 0.8% of patients with OHS. If these scars develop within the macula, there is a 25% chance of developing maculopathy with subsequent vision loss within 3 years. Optic atrophy, cataract, and peripheral retinal degeneration are not features of OHS.

question: For a patient positive for HLA-A29 and whose fundus and ﬂuorescein angiogram are shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

explanation: The characteristic appearance of birdshot chorioretinopathy is multiple creamy, subretinal lesions appearing to radiate from the optic nerve, as demonstrated by this patient. Symptoms may include decreased vision (potentially due to macular edema), photopsias, and other subjective visual disturbance. Carriers of the HLA-A29 genotype have a relative risk of 80 to 100 times compared to the risk of noncarriers. The vitreous inﬁltrate is typically less pronounced than in the other conditions mentioned. Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome is typically unilateral, and Harada syndrome typically exhibits more prominent vitreous inﬂammation. The ﬂuorescein angiogram shows cystoid macular edema, which is rarely associated with APMPPE. In addition, APMPPE may be associated with HLA B27 or HLA DR2 but is not associated with HLA-A29.

question: What cell type produces antibodies?
explanation: Antibodies, or immunoglobulins, are produced by plasma cells derived from B lymphocytes after appropriate antigenic stimulation with T- lymphocyte help. Plasma cells initially secrete IgM antibodies, followed later by production of other isotypes after antibody-class switching. Antibodies are released into the eﬀerent lymph ﬂuid, draining into the venous circulation. Once bound to their speciﬁc epitope, antibodies mediate a variety of immune eﬀector activities, including opsonization for phagocytosis and complement activation via the classical pathway.

question: A child with a history of yellow-red skin lesions presents with unilateral recurrent hyphema. A few iris nodules are noted. What histologic ﬁndings would be expected on skin or iris biopsy?

options.C: large histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and Touton giant cells

explanation: The case described clinically resembles juvenile xanthogranuloma, which may feature yellow-red skin lesions. Intraocular features may include recurrent hyphema. A biopsy of a skin or iris nodule would be expected to feature large histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and Touton giant cells. Necrosis with formation of pseudorosettes can be seen in retinoblastoma. Bilateral diﬀuse uveal melanocytic proliferation is characterized by inﬁltration of the uveal tract by benign nevoid or spindle-shaped cells. Caseating granulomas are a feature of tuberculous granulomas, but tuberculous uveitis does not feature recurrent hyphemas.

question: In a patient with anterior chamber and vitreous cells and macular edema, what information would best help support a diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa (RP)?
explanation: Patients with RP often have variable numbers of vitreous and anterior chamber cells and can develop macular edema. Features of RP that diﬀerentiate it from uveitis include nyctalopia, positive family history, and, on fundus examination, waxy disc pallor, attenuation of arterioles, and a bone-spicule pattern of pigmentary changes in the mid- periphery. Electroretinographic (ERG) responses of patients with RP often appear severely depressed or extinguished. However, these ﬁndings can be seen in late posterior uveitis, making diﬀerentiation between the entities very diﬃcult in some cases.

question: What test is most appropriate in the initial workup of a patient with uveitis suspected of having sarcoidosis?
explanation: Chest x-ray is the single best screening modality for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis, as it reveals abnormalities in approximately 90% of patients who have sarcoidosis. The classic feature of a chest x-ray (CXR) in this setting is hilar lymphadenopathy, although chest computed tomography (CT) may also reveal mediastinal and other parenchymal abnormalities. Although retinal angiography may reveal leakage from retinal vasculitis (technically, retinal phlebitis), retinal vasculitis is not speciﬁc to sarcoidosis and can be seen in several other posterior uveitides. ANA and CRP have no screening value for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis. Chest abnormalities are present at some point in up to 90% of sarcoid patients, but these do not persist throughout the disease course and thus maybe absent at the time of workup. question: Nonsteroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) reduce the incidence of macular edema after cataract surgery by reducing the inﬂammatory mediators of what pathway?
explanation: The cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway produces prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and prostacyclins. Prostaglandins may be the cause of uveitic macular edema, in association with anterior segment surgery or inﬂammation. Posterior diﬀusion of 1 or more of the eicosanoids BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What antimetabolite is most commonly associated with hepatic toxicity?
explanation: Although any antimetabolite can be associated with hepatic toxicity, methotrexate is most commonly associated with it. Often the elevation of liver enzyme levels is modest and reversible on holding the medication or decreasing the dose. Rarely, the liver damage can be severe and persistent, with resultant signiﬁcant morbidity. Reversible hepatic toxicity occurs in 15% of patients on methotrexate, as opposed BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: For a patient less than 6 years old with unilateral pseudohypopyon, what is the primary concern when considering an aqueous or vitreous aspirate?

options.B: risk of vitreous wicking and/or cataractogenesis
options.D: risk of dispersing malignant retinoblastoma cells

explanation: Retinoblastoma, especially the variant of diﬀuse inﬁltrating retinoblastoma, may present with anterior chamber cells, pseudohypopyon that shifts with change of head position, or vitreous opacity and other signs of inﬂammation, but lack the typical calciﬁcation usually seen with this tumor. Aspiration can be diagnostic, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Within what ethnic group or geographic region is birdshot chorioretinopathy most prevalent?
explanation: Birdshot chorioretinopathy is most prevalent in individuals of northern European descent. Typically diagnosed in the fourth to sixth decade of life, this entity aﬀects women more frequently than men.

question: What mediator plays a role in anterior chamber–associated immune deviation (ACAID)?
explanation: Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) play roles as regulators of ACAID. Interferon gamma causes neutrophil and macrophage inﬁltration. Substance P plays a role in vascular permeability and causes leukocyte inﬁltration. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha is involved in mononuclear cell inﬁltration.

question: What is the most likely explanation for his elevated intraocular pressure?
explanation: There are several "lens-induced" glaucomas; 3 are secondary open- angle (phacoantigenic [previously termed phacoanaphylactic], phacolytic, lens-particle), and 1 is secondary angle-closure (phacomorphic). Phacoantigenic uveitis is a form of uveitis that develops when a patient is sensitized to his or her own lens protein. It often occurs in a posttraumatic setting, with disruption of the lens capsule. Since the immune sensitization does not involve immunoglobulin E (IgE), the stem “anaphylaxis” of the older term, phacoanaphylactic, is confusing. The presentation of phacoantigenic uveitis is of a granulomatous uveitis (ie, large, “greasy" or "mutton-fat” keratic precipitates, iris nodules). In this vignette, the mature cataract and keratic precipitates are suggestive of violation of the lens capsule and associated phacoantigenic uveitis. Phacolytic uveitis, also termed phacolytic glaucoma, is a complication of a mature or hypermature (liqueﬁed) cataract that results in the leaking of lens proteins through an intact lens capsule. Typical ﬁndings include cells, ﬂare, and lens-engorged macrophages settled in the inferior trabecular meshwork. In contrast to phacoantigenic/phacoanaphylactic uveitis, there are usually no keratic precipitates or synechiae present. Lens particle glaucoma results from fragments of cortical lens obstructing the trabecular meshwork. In phacomorphic glaucoma, an enlarging or intumescent cataract grows in the anterior-posterior dimension and thus pushes the iris forward, leading to angle closure.

question: A 52-year-old man presents with bilateral panuveitis and retinal vasculitis. He also has complaints of arthralgia, diplopia, diarrhea, and poor performance at work. What test may help with the diagnosis?
explanation: Whipple disease is a rare multisystem disease caused by the Tropheryma whipplei bacterium. It is most common in middle-aged white men. Migratory arthritis occurs in 80% of cases, and diarrhea, steatorrhea, and malabsorption occur in 75%. Central nervous system involvement occurs in 10% of cases and results in seizures, dementia, and coma. Neuro-ophthalmic signs can include cranial nerve palsies, nystagmus, and ophthalmoplegia. Intraocular involvement occurs in less than 5% of cases. Patients can present with bilateral panuveitis, retinal vasculitis, and multifocal chorioretinitis. The gold standard for diagnosis of Whipple disease is a duodenal biopsy that demonstrates a periodic acid–Schiﬀ–positive bacillus in macrophages within intestinal villi. 50 per pa.

question: What is the preferred medium for culturing mycobacteria?
explanation: Aerobic bacteria grow best on blood agar, chocolate agar, and in thioglycollate broth. Mycobacteria grow on blood agar and Löwenstein-Jensen agar. (Middlebrook agar is also used, however this is not listed in the BCSC). question: A patient has decreased vision from a vitreous hemorrhage, and no retinal breaks can be found. After the hemorrhage clears, the retinal appearance is abnormal, as shown in the image. What is the most likely systemic diagnosis?
explanation: The image depicts an area of midperipheral venous sheathing and sclerosis, suggestive of a systemic vasculitis. Among the answer choices given (including toxoplasmosis, ankylosing spondylitis, and Bartonella henselae infection), ANCA-associated vasculitis is the only one that suggests the presence of a systemic vasculitis.

question: A patient with Vogt-Koyanagi- Harada (VKH) syndrome experienced resolution of bilateral serous retinal detachments with oral corticosteroid therapy. Six months later, the patient's visual acuity is 20/25 in both eyes. However, despite prednisolone acetate 1 drops every 2 hours and prednisone 20 mg/day orally, the patient is still plagued with persistent active anterior uveitis (2+ cells) in both eyes. What is the best next step in the treatment of this patient's condition?

explanation: Even though VKH syndrome is usually responsive to corticosteroid therapy, patients may experience recurrent episodes of inﬂammation. It is not safe nor recommended to use systemic corticosteroids on a long-term basis, so if there is recurrent inﬂammation, steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy should be considered. question: What test is likely to be positive in a 42-year-old patient with recurrent scleritis, proptosis, and a recent history of severe sinus disease?
explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly, Wegener granulomatosis), is a multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by the classic triad of necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower respiratory tract, focal segmental glomerulonephritis, and necrotizing vasculitis of small arteries and veins. Involvement of the paranasal sinuses is the most characteristic clinical feature of this disorder, followed by pulmonary and renal disease. Ocular or orbital involvement is found in 15% of patients at presentation and in up to 50% of patients during the course of the disease. Orbital involvement, one of the most frequently reported ocular ﬁndings, is usually secondary to contiguous extension of the granulomatous inﬂammatory process from the paranasal sinuses into the orbit. ANCA are antibodies directed against cytoplasmic azurophilic granules of neutrophils and monocytes that are speciﬁc markers for a group of related systemic vasculitides, including GPA, MPA, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome), renal limited vasculitis, and pauci-immunoglomerulonephritis. The cytoplasmic, or c-ANCA, pattern is both sensitive and speciﬁc for GPA and is present in up to 95% of patients; proteinase 3 is the most common target antigen (referred to as PR3-ANCA). The patient here is unlikely to have thyroid disease based on the presented ﬁndings. HLA-B27-associated uveitis would not present with scleritis and proptosis. Birdshot chorioretinopathy has strong association with HLA-A29, the strongest association between a disease and HLA class I documented gene (85%-97.5% of patients are HLA-A29-positive). These patients usually have posterior segment disease rather than scleritis.

question: What is the recommended treatment for a patient with choroidal candidiasis without vitreous involvement?

options.A: oral ﬂuconazole and pars plana vitrectomy

explanation: When hematogenous dissemination of Candida involves only the choroid, oral triazole antifungals (voriconazole or ﬂuconazole) are eﬀective. When the vitreous is involved, intravitreal antifungals (voriconazole or amphotericin B) should be given, often in conjunction with pars plana vitrectomy. Oral voriconazole for this particular case is the best option, given that it will have excellent intraocular penetration, and there is no vitreous involvement at this time, so vitrectomy is not required. question: What common side eﬀect is unique to cyclophosphamide among immunomodulatory therapies used in treating uveitis?
explanation: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent that works to impair DNA replication by alkylating purines in DNA and RNA, thereby inducing cell death. Compared to other immunomodulatory agents, alkylating agents, including cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil, have a higher risk of inducing a malignancy, particularly hematologic malignancies such as polycythemia rubra vera. A unique side eﬀect of cyclophosphamide is hemorrhagic cystitis, which is more common with BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What systemic disease has the strongest association for uveitis with positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA)?
explanation: The presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) has the strongest association for uveitis in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). The type of JIA-associated uveitis where ANA is positive is the pauciarticular type BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What risk factor in a patient with West Nile virus (WNV)-associated uveitis is associated with an increased risk of WNV-associated mortality?
explanation: Diabetes mellitus and advanced age in someone with West Nile virus (WNV)-associated uveitis are associated with the development of severe neurologic disease (meningitis or encephalitis). In addition, diabetes mellitus has been implicated as a risk factor for WNV-related death. Systemically, a patient may present with fever, myalgias, headache, conjunctivitis, and a maculopapular rash. Cardiomyopathy has not been associated with an increased risk of WNV-associated mortality.

question: What is the immunologic mechanism for type IV hypersensitivity?

options.A: Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity triggers apoptosis of epidermal keratocytes.
options.B: Activation of IgE receptors on eosinophils results in release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other inﬂammatory mediators.
options.C: Recognition of antigen by memory T cells results in activation and ampliﬁcation of clones that react to the speciﬁc antigen still present in the skin.
options.D: Deposition of antigen-antibody immune complexes results in activation of complement and attracts tissue macrophages.

explanation: A prototypical type 4 delayed hypersensitivity reaction is poison ivy– related contact dermatitis. Upon ﬁrst exposure to urushiol oil, the agent that causes this dermatitis, the antigen is taken to regional lymph nodes by antigen-presenting cells. Once lymphocytes are found that recognize this antigen, they enter the circulation, but only after the antigen is no longer found in the skin. Subsequent exposures, however, result in activation of memory lymphocytes that produce clinical signs of inﬂammation within 24 to 36 hours. IgE mediates allergic-type immune reactions, and antigen antibody immune complexes mediate serum sickness and may be part of the immunopathogenesis of vasculitis. Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity is a mechanism of removing infected or neoplastic cells. It is caused by sarcoidosis.

question: A new patient presents for assessment of uveitis with a calciﬁc band in the interpalpebral zone. What does that tell you about the patient's uveitis?
explanation: Calciﬁc band keratopathy develops in patients with chronic uveitis over years. question: Aside from eﬀector blockade and anterior chamber–associated immune deviation, what is the major mechanism that aﬀords immune privilege to the cornea?
explanation: Cytokines and complement help recruit immune mediators to the central cornea, which is otherwise relatively devoid of immune eﬀectors. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue is responsible for conjunctival antigenic processing, but the eﬀector limb of this system can spill over onto the corneal surface and recruit immune eﬀectors to the cornea. Limbal physiology is the mechanism that keeps immune eﬀectors from reaching the central cornea (ie, makes the cornea immune privileged), mainly by serving as a barrier to vascularization of the cornea, which would provide great immune access to the central cornea, but at the cost of severe reduction in vision.

question: What is the most common infectious cause of a unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis with lymphadenopathy?
explanation: Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, or granulomatous conjunctivitis and ipsilateral lymphadenopathy, is typically associated with Bartonella infection, or cat scratch disease. Francisella tularensis, the organism responsible for tularemia, is also a possible etiology, as are syphilis, tuberculosis, and sporotrichosis, but these are all uncommon. Adult chlamydial inclusion conjunctivitis may be considered but the conjunctival reaction is follicular rather than granulomatous. Streptococcus does not cause a granulomatous conjunctivitis.

question: Histoplasma capsulatum infection most commonly occurs in what geographic area?
explanation: The highest prevalence of H capsulatum exposure is in the Mississippi and Ohio River watersheds. Although the Missouri River is a branch of the Mississippi, H capsulatum has not been found endemic to its valley. Coccidioidomycosis, which can be found in the San Joaquin Valley as well as in the soil of several southwestern states, Mexico, and Central and South America, may mimic the clinical features of presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome ("punched-out" small chorioretinal scars, peripapillary scarring). This disorder is due to the fungus Coccidioides, not H capsulatum. The Hudson River valley is devoid of H capsulatum.

question: What histologic ﬁnding is associated with Vogt-Koyanagi- Harada (VKH) syndrome?
explanation: Dalen-Fuchs nodules are collections of epithelioid histiocytes and lymphocytes between Bruch membrane and the RPE. They can be seen in sympathetic ophthalmia and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome. In VKH syndrome, the entire choroid, including the choriocapillaris, is typically involved by the inﬂammatory process; relative sparing of the choriocapillaris is characteristic of sympathetic ophthalmia. question: An ophthalmologist is consulted about a man who has polyarthritis, diarrhea, altered mentation, and blurry vision. The ocular examination is notable for bilateral panuveitis, retinal vasculitis, and pendular vergence motions concurrent with mastication. What is the preferred treatment for the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pendular vergence movements coinciding with mastication is descriptive of oculomasticatory myorhythmia, which is pathognomonic for Whipple disease. Whipple disease is a rare infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei, and the gold standard for diagnosis is a duodenal biopsy with periodic acid–Schiﬀ (PAS) staining. There is central nervous system involvement in approximately 10% of cases of Whipple disease, although intraocular involvement is rare, at approximately 5% of cases. Other possible manifestations of uveitis associated with Whipple disease include multifocal chorioretinitis and vitritis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment for this infection, although ceftriaxone or tetracycline are possible alternative therapies.

question: Once the diagnosis of sympathetic ophthalmia is established, what is the preferred initial management?

options.C: intraocular injection of foscarnet to the sympathizing eye
options.D: panretinal laser photocoagulation to the sympathizing eye

explanation: In the rare instances when sympathetic ophthalmia does follow either injury or surgery, standard treatments such as corticosteroids almost always control the inﬂammation. Therefore, enucleation or evisceration of an injured eye to minimize risk of sympathetic ophthalmia should be undertaken only when the eye is painful, structurally disorganized, and has no light perception. Panretinal photocoagulation has no place in managing this form of uveitis. Foscarnet is an antiviral antibiotic that is used to treat cytomegalovirus or other herpes viral retinitis, such as in acute retinal BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What would be the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue the steroid taper slowly and reassure the patient that this type of inﬂammation "burns out" with time.
options.B: Increase topical corticosteroids and initiate therapy with an antimetabolite (eg, methotrexate).
options.C: Increase topical corticosteroids and initiate therapy with oral acetazolamide.
options.D: Schedule the patient for glaucoma valve placement.

explanation: Although her increasing intraocular pressure is a concern, there are other options available to help control her intraocular inﬂammation and pressure, while avoiding surgery. On the other hand, simply increasing her topical corticosteroid and starting oral acetazolamide will only serve to temporize the same issue: namely, the patient needs a steroid- sparing agent to keep her intraocular inﬂammation under control and spare her the side eﬀects of steroids. Tapering the steroid and providing reassurance is incorrect, given that the patient's inﬂammation has ﬂared up when the ophthalmologist has tried to taper the dosing below 4 times per day. The correct option here would be to increase the topical corticosteroids to get her inﬂammation back under control, start some form of immunomodulatory therapy (typically an antimetabolite to start with) to maintain control of her inﬂammation while tapering the steroid, and manage her intraocular pressure during this time.

question: What is the most common ocular manifestation of human T-cell lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1) infection?
explanation: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus of Oncovirinae. It is endemic in Japan, Central and South America, and the Caribbean Islands. Most cases of HTLV-1 uveitis are intermediate uveitis. Other ocular manifestations are keratoconjunctivitis sicca, retinal inﬁltrates, and optic neuropathy. central cornea and sclera A. 85%.

question: What external structures of an otherwise healthy eye do not typically contain antigen- presenting cells?
explanation: There are no antigen-presenting cells found in either the central cornea or the sclera in a healthy eye. The paracentral cornea and central cornea are normally devoid of antigen-presenting cells and avascular. Various stimuli such as trauma, infection, or certain cytokines can recruit antigen-presenting cells. Plasma-derived proteins such as complement, IgM, and IgG are present in moderate concentrations in the peripheral cornea. Langerhans cells are typically found in vascularized areas, such as the conjunctiva and the limbus. Macrophages can also be found within the conjunctiva. Langerhans cells are a subset of dendritic cells that are present in most human epithelial cells. Their main function is acting as accessory immunoregulatory cells that process and present antigens to T lymphocytes through the MHC class II molecule. By presenting processed antigens, they activate and initiate a response from the lymphocytes.

question: What is a major risk factor for the development of primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) and primary intraocular lymphoma?

options.B: history of central nervous system irradiation

explanation: The most signiﬁcant risk factor for the development of primary intraocular lymphoma and primary CNS lymphomas is immunodeﬁciency. This includes HIV infection (which increases the risk from 50- to 500-fold), iatrogenic immune suppression, and aging (half of all cases occur after 60 years of age). The incidence of PCNSL appears to be increasing and is projected to occur in 1 of every 100,000 immunocompetent patients.

question: What systemic disease should be considered in a previously healthy adult patient from Mexico with uveitis, seizures, and calciﬁcations in the central nervous system (CNS) on computed tomography (CT) scan?
explanation: Cysticercosis is the most common ocular tapeworm infection caused by Taenia solium, which is endemic to Mexico, Central and South America, Eastern Europe, Africa, and India. The eye and CNS are commonly aﬀected. It may involve the eye and the adnexae. Subretinal space may harbor the parasite. These larvae may cause exudative retinal detachment, perforate the retina, and invade the vitreous cavity. Larvae can be seen undulating in the vitreous or subretinal space. Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures and, less commonly, headaches. In developing countries, this is one of the most common causes of seizures. Cysts located within the ventricles of the brain can block the outﬂow of cerebrospinal ﬂuid and present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. SSPE is a fatal, progressive degenerative disease of the central nervous BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What immunosuppressive drug used to treat noninfectious ocular inﬂammation is most clearly associated with an increased risk of malignancy?
explanation: Alkylating agents include cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil. The most worrisome adverse eﬀect of these agents is an increased risk of malignancy. There drugs should be used with great caution. Azathioprine and methotrexate are antimetabolites, and cyclosporine is a T-cell inhibitor. The Systemic Immunosuppressive Therapy for Eye Diseases (SITE) cohort study of 7957 patients with noninfectious uveitis showed that patients who took azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, or systemic corticosteroids had overall cancer mortality rates similar to those who never took those medications. There was a non-statistically signiﬁcant increase in cancer-related mortality rates in patients treated with cyclophosphamide.

question: What is the most common fundus autoﬂuorescence (FAF) imaging pattern in a patient with multifocal choroiditis?

options.B: multiple punctate hypoautoﬂuorescent spots that may be more numerous than clinical appearance
options.C: hyperautoﬂuorescent areas that correspond to areas of blockage on ﬂuorescein angiogram (FA)

explanation: The most common fundus autoﬂuorescence ﬁnding in multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis is multiple punctate hypoautoﬂuorescent spots. Some spots correspond to areas of chorioretinal atrophy, but many more spots may be discerned than are visible on fundus examination. question: Sympathetic ophthalmia can be diﬀerentiated from Vogt-Koyanagi- Harada (VKH) syndrome by what feature?
explanation: Aside from a history of penetrating ocular trauma, sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) and VKH-associated uveitis are essentially identical, as both can manifest meningeal signs (although meningeal signs typically present after ocular inﬂammation in SO, whereas they precede ocular inﬂammation in VKH), both are bilateral, both respond well to corticosteroids, and both represent an autoimmune response to tissue pigment. question: For what form of uveitis is aspiration and laboratory examination of a patient's intraocular ﬂuid most likely to lead to a speciﬁc diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: a patient with chronic unilateral anterior uveitis
options.B: a patient with retinitis and vitritis
options.C: a patient with chronic bilateral anterior uveitis
options.D: a 14-year-old patient with sudden- onset bilateral anterior uveitis and acute interstitial nephritis

explanation: There are many infectious etiologies of retinitis, and the clinical appearance is sometimes nonspeciﬁc. In immunosuppressed patients, such as those with HIV and AIDS, the diﬀerential is even more broad. Most patients with viral retinitis will have infection secondary to one of the herpes viruses, such as herpes simplex 1 or 2 (HSV-1 or -2) or varicella zoster virus (VZV). However, Candida, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Toxoplasma gondii must also be considered in the appropriate scenario. Diagnostic aspiration of intraocular ﬂuid with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing can clarify the diagnosis. Chronic bilateral anterior uveitis is unlikely to be infectious in origin, although CMV, HSV, tuberculosis, leprosy, or other rare infections should also be considered if the history or examination suggests one of these diseases. A chronic unilateral anterior uveitis is more likely to be infectious than a bilateral case, due to the more frequent inclusion of HSV in this category, but in general is unlikely to be infectious in origin, and therefore diagnostic aspiration of intraocular ﬂuid is infrequently indicated. In a patient with acute interstitial nephritis and bilateral anterior uveitis, the presumptive diagnosis is the tubulointerstitial nephritis uveitis (TINU) syndrome, which does not require intraocular ﬂuid for diagnosis. Syphilis, which is on the diﬀerential for all of the etiologies discussed, is diagnosed with treponemal serum antibodies, and does not require intraocular ﬂuid.

question: In a patient with multifocal choroiditis, what is the preferred management of chronic inﬂammation?

options.D: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy

explanation: Multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis is an idiopathic inﬂammatory disorder of choroid, retina, and vitreous. It is more common in young, myopic women. It presents with photopsias, enlarged physiologic blind spot, and decreased vision. Because this is a chronic, recurrent inﬂammatory disease, immunomodulatory therapy with steroids or steroid-sparing agents is recommended. A viral etiology with herpes simplex and Epstein-Barr virus has been suggested but not veriﬁed; antiviral therapy is not used. Intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs are important adjuncts for the treatment of CNV. There is no role of cryotherapy.

question: For a patient with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), also known as juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA), what combination of laboratory ﬁndings would indicate the greatest risk of developing iritis?
explanation: The group of JRA (or JIA) patients with the greatest likelihood of developing uveitis are those with positive ANA and negative RF results. The group with the lowest likelihood of developing uveitis, and therefore a decreased frequency of screening required, are those with the presence of RF without ANA antibodies, such as in Still disease. ANCA are antibodies directed against cytoplasmic azurophilic granules of neutrophils and monocytes that are speciﬁc markers for a group of related systemic vasculitides, including GPA, MPA, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome), renal limited vasculitis, and pauci- immunoglomerulonephritis. HLA-B27 is a major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I antigen present in approximately 6.1% of the US general population. It is strongly associated with acute anterior uveitis, ankylosing spondylitis, and reactive arthritis syndrome.

question: What test commonly gives a false- positive result in patients with leptospirosis?
explanation: False positives with the puriﬁed protein derivative (PPD) can occur in a patient who has had a prior bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination, atypical mycobacterial infections, and bladder cancer. Interferon gamma release assays (IGRAs) are much less frequently associated with false positives compared to PPD in the setting of prior BCG vaccination. Urine histoplasmin antigen testing is carried out when there is suspicion for Histoplasma capsulatum infection. False positives are rare. question: A patient with a mature, white cataract develops anterior chamber inﬂammation and an elevated IOP. If the lens capsule has not been penetrated or traumatized, what is the most likely mechanism of inﬂammation and increased pressure?

options.A: zonal granuloma surrounding the capsule shifting the iris forward
options.B: lens crystallin–inducing prostaglandin synthesis in the ciliary body
options.C: direct lens protein blockade of the trabecular meshwork
options.D: clogging of the trabecular meshwork by macrophages engorged with lens proteins

explanation: Phacolytic glaucoma and uveitis is the result of lens protein leaking through an intact capsule, typically in a hypermature cataract. Macrophages scavenge the protein from the anterior chamber, occlude the trabecular meshwork, and result in an elevated IOP. Delamination of the lens capsule is a feature of exfoliation syndrome, not phacolytic uveitis. Zonal granulomas are a histopathological inﬂammatory ﬁnding in a disrupted or traumatized lens, surrounding the site of capsule injury; in contrast, in cases of phacolytic glaucoma the capsule is presumably intact.

question: A 69-year-old woman who had cataract surgery 3 months ago has had several episodes of inﬂammation each time her topical corticosteroids have been tapered. She now has a hypopyon and an iris mass, necrotizing scleritis, and vitreous snowballs. What type of organism is most likely causative?
explanation: Recurrent inﬂammation in an eye that has previously undergone surgery is concerning for chronic postoperative endophthalmitis. Chronic postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by Propionibacterium acnes, a gram-positive anaerobe. Other gram-positive bacteria, gram-negative bacteria, Mycobacterium species, and fungi, such as Candida parapsilosis, Aspergillus ﬂavus, and Torulopsis candida, can also cause chronic postoperative endophthalmitis. While chronic postoperative fungal endophthalmitis may present similarly to a bacterial infection, certain clinical signs make a fungal etiology more likely, including a corneal inﬁltrate or edema, mass in the iris or ciliary body, necrotizing scleritis, vitreous snowballs, or a "string-of-pearls" appearance in the vitreous.

question: How does the Fas ligand function to create immune privilege in the eye?

options.A: downregulates major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecule expression in the cornea
options.C: blocks antigen-presenting cells (APC) in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)
options.D: triggers apoptosis of lymphocytes expressing Fas receptor

explanation: The Fas ligand is constitutively expressed in the iris and corneal endothelium. It triggers apoptosis of lymphocytes expressing the Fas receptor and is one of the most important mechanisms of eﬀector blockage contributing to immune privilege in the eye. MHC molecule expression is normally low in the corneal stroma, and increased expression has been linked to corneal graft rejection.
